facts.fact: Newly hatched Artemia (instar I nauplii) do not feed and live on their yolk reserves; they start feeding after molting to instar II.
Nauplii from decapsulated cysts have roughly 30-55% more energy and individual weight than regular instar I nauplii, depending on strain.
Newly hatched nauplii from decapsulated cysts are more nutritious because they spend no energy breaking out of the shell.
Newly hatched nauplii lack a complete digestive system and cannot be enriched until about 24 hours old.
Enrichment: move nauplii aged 24 hours to a separate container and enrich for 12 to 24 hours with a HUFA booster such as Selco.
Adding HUFA boosters to a tub of adult brine shrimp spoils the water and may kill the shrimp; enrich in a separate container.
Artemia hatching water is best kept at 25-28°C; below 25°C cysts hatch more slowly and above 33°C their metabolism stops irreversibly.
Keep hatching water pH above 8 and oxygen above 2 mg/l, preferably 5 mg/l.
Give about 2000 lux of light at the water surface, at least in the first hours after the cysts are fully hydrated.
Use up to 5 g of cysts per litre in volumes under 20 l, and at most 2 g/l in larger volumes.
At 33 g/l salinity and 25°C, the first nauplii appear after about 12-16 h and most should have hatched within 24 h.
Hatched Artemia take about 24 hours to hatch and roughly 24 more hours to reach instar II, when they can take in food.
Keep strong, continuous aeration from an airline reaching the bottom of the hatcher; decapsulated cysts need a lot of bubbles to avoid clumping.
Seahorse.org decapsulation: hydrate 2 tsp cysts in 2 cups lukewarm water with aeration for one hour, then add 2/3 cup of regular bleach.
During bleaching the cysts turn from brown to light gray to orange; stop when mostly orange, pour into a net, rinse with cold water and add dechlorinator (sodium thiosulfate).
Over-bleaching cysts during decapsulation stops them from hatching.
The decapsulation reaction gives off heat; the solution must never go above 40°C, and embryos must not stay in it longer than necessary.
Rinse decapsulated cysts until no bleach smell remains and store them sealed in the fridge; they still work well for about a week.
Unhatched cysts and empty shells cannot be digested and may block the gut of the larvae that eat them.
With normal (not decapsulated) cysts, nauplii cannot always be completely separated from their shells; decapsulated cysts avoid this.
Unenriched Artemia generally does not work well for seahorse fry, so newly hatched brine shrimp is not a complete food for every fry.
Tubifex worms live in sediments of lakes and rivers and sometimes in sewer lines.
Tubifex harvested from sewers, open water or hatcheries may carry diseases, and can be vectors of whirling disease of salmonids.
Keeping tubifex under brisk running water until they empty their guts only partly reduces disease risk; a strong stream also washes off mud.
Tubifex are very fattening and low in some essential amino acids; fish fed mostly on them may grow fast but be less healthy and less colourful.
Some fish, such as Rift Valley cichlids, may overeat tubifex until they become sick.
In poorly kept aquaria, uneaten tubifex can become a pest that carpets the bottom.
Trùn chỉ (tubificid worms) include Tubifex tubifex, Limnodrilus hoffmeisteri and Branchiura sowerbyi, about 20-25 mm long with 55-95 segments.
Tubifex tubifex contains about 57% protein, 13.3% fat, 2.04% fiber and 3.6% ash.
In Vietnam, tubificid worms live at high density in wastewater channels, ponds and freshwater lakes, and are cultured as live food for larval eels, catfish and ornamental fish.
Bloodworms (trùng huyết) are larvae of midges in the family Chironomidae; red ones carry a pigment that helps them survive in low-oxygen water.
Transparent chironomid larvae are sold as glassworms; red ones are bloodworms.
Bloodworms on a dry-weight basis contain 47.7–62.5% protein and 4.9–28.6% fat, and are a good iron source.
Large imported frozen bloodworms have hard, bristled exoskeletons that can clog the gut of fish with small intestinal openings, such as discus, rainbowfish and some tetras.
Bloodworm chitin is hard for young fry to digest because they develop the enzyme chitinase later; this has caused deaths in some post-larvae.
Some rainbowfish with swollen bellies or gut obstructions have been linked to bloodworm feeding.
Handling bloodworm foods has caused allergies in some hobbyists, such as conjunctivitis, rhinitis, asthma or hives; mostly in people who handle them often.
In an informal 2018 survey of 445 readers, 34% reported a known or suspected bloodworm allergy, and the median time to a first reaction was four years.
To limit bloodworm allergy, use gloves or feeding tongs, or buy portioned frozen cubes that need no handling; face masks may help with dust.
Bloodworm dust is described as the worst trigger; some keepers say freeze-dried worms caused more reactions than frozen ones (anecdotal).
Anyone with symptoms after handling bloodworms should seek medical advice; severe reactions can need emergency care.
Moina suit freshwater fry: newly hatched fry of most freshwater species can eat young Moina as their first food.
Moina reach much higher densities than Daphnia; average daily yield is 106–110 g/m3, three to four times Daphnia's.
Moina tolerate high temperatures and a wide range of oxygen levels.
Moina can quickly grow too large for fry to eat, and dense hopping adults can harass and damage fry.
Passing Moina through 500-micron mesh to sort them tends to break the animals apart.
Batch culture of Moina starts a new culture in a separate container every day, which keeps cultures free of contaminants.
A keeper reports feeding tubifex to betta fry from about two weeks old, after soaking the clump and separating the worms with tweezers.
A keeper reports that leaving tubifex in a basket (rọ) or clump let bigger betta fry dominate, giving uneven growth and fry with long beaks and oversized spoon heads.
A keeper reports better results spreading worms evenly over the whole fry tank and feeding often, day and night.
Vietnamese keepers call brine shrimp "artemia", cysts "bào nang", the larvae "ấu trùng artemia", and decapsulation "tách vỏ (trứng)".
"Bobo" is a Vietnamese shop name for small freshwater plankton fed live, also called "trứng nước" or "bo bo nước ngọt" (water fleas such as Moina/Daphnia).
Trùng huyết (also written trùn huyết) is sold in Vietnam fresh and frozen; shops describe it as a mud-dwelling mosquito larva, though it is a chironomid midge larva.
